description: M13 — CPS Transform & Concurrency Primitives: Full CPS compiler transform with suspension inference, user-facing spawn/await/parallel/race primitives, Future type, direct-style suspension propagation, VM stack root removal, adaptive GC threshold, OOM escalation, plus comprehensive .jacl e2e test coverage for M13 concurrency and M11 type system gaps.

userStories.title: Future type and GC integration
userStories.description: As a developer, I need a Future value type so that spawn can return a handle that await uses to suspend and resume, and the GC can trace futures and their waiters.
acceptanceCriteria: Add JACL_TAG_FUTURE to the value tag enum in value.c

Define JaclFuture struct: { _Atomic uint32_t state (PENDING/RESOLVED/ERROR), _Atomic uint64_t result (JaclVal), FutureWaiter* waiters (linked list), synchronization for waiter registration vs resolution race }
Define FutureWaiter struct: { JaclVal continuation, FutureWaiter* next }
Add OBJ_FUTURE and OBJ_FUTURE_WAITER to GCObjType enum in gc.c
Allocate futures via gc_alloc(heap, OBJ_FUTURE, sizeof(JaclFuture)); waiter nodes via gc_alloc(heap, OBJ_FUTURE_WAITER, sizeof(FutureWaiter))
GC trace for OBJ_FUTURE: trace result (if resolved/errored) and traverse waiters list (each continuation closure). GC trace for OBJ_FUTURE_WAITER: trace continuation + next pointer
jacl_future(ThreadHeap*) constructor creates pending future, returns JaclVal
jacl_future_resolve(JaclFuture*, JaclVal result) atomically sets result + RESOLVED state, returns waiter list for caller to schedule
jacl_future_error(JaclFuture*, JaclVal error) same as resolve but ERROR state

jacl_future_add_waiter(JaclFuture*, JaclVal continuation, ThreadHeap*) — if pending, prepend waiter node return true; if already resolved/errored, return false (caller schedules continuation immediately)
jacl_is_future(JaclVal) predicate and future? builtin in VM
Write barrier on resolution: gc_write_barrier(old=JACL_NIL, new=result) when storing result into future
Unit tests: create/resolve/error futures, waiter registration on pending and already-resolved futures, GC traces live future with waiters
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: JaclFuture is a mutable container like atom — uses atomic state/result fields. Waiter list is GC-managed (no malloc). The mutex/spinlock per future only contends during the resolve-vs-add_waiter race window. Most futures have 0-1 waiters.

userStories.title: Suspension analysis in compiler
userStories.description: As a developer, I need the compiler to determine which procedures can suspend so the CPS transform knows which procs to rewrite and illegal suspension contexts produce compile-time errors.
acceptanceCriteria: Add bool suspends field to Local, GlobalArity, and Upvalue structs in compiler.c

Implement pre-compilation suspension analysis pass: (1) walk all proc/fn definitions in AST including nested, (2) mark procs directly containing await/parallel/race as suspending, (3) propagate transitively — any proc calling a known-suspending proc becomes suspending, (4) iterate until fixpoint
Store suspension map (proc name -> suspends) for use during compilation
During compilation, look up callee's suspension status when resolving calls and propagate to enclosing proc
Indirect calls to closures with unknown suspension status: conservatively assume suspending (enclosing proc gets CPS-transformed). Safe — may over-transform but never misses a suspension point
Compile-time error: suspension point inside a closure passed to non-suspending higher-order builtin (map, filter, reduce, each) — 'cannot suspend inside non-suspending callback'
Compile-time error: suspending closure passed as argument to non-suspending higher-order builtin
Compile-time error: suspension point inside try/catch block — 'cannot suspend inside try/catch; use error capture on futures instead'
spawn is NOT a suspension point — can appear in any proc. Calling a suspending proc automatically propagates suspension to the caller (direct style)

Unit tests: suspension inferred for direct use, transitive calls, nested procs; indirect call to unknown closure conservatively suspending; compile errors for illegal contexts (try/catch, non-suspending callback)
All existing tests pass (build.sh) — no existing code uses suspension points, all procs inferred non-suspending
userStories.notes: The fixpoint analysis is a separate pass before full compilation. It walks AST command nodes looking for await/parallel/race head strings, then propagates. Convergence is fast — most procs don't suspend. Worst case O(N^2) for N proc definitions, acceptable for typical program sizes.

userStories.title: CPS transform — sequential code
userStories.description: As a developer, I need the compiler to transform suspending procedures with sequential suspension points into continuation-closure chains, so that await can suspend and resume via continuations.
acceptanceCriteria: CPS-transformed suspending procs take a hidden continuation parameter __k — the result continuation called with the proc's final result instead of returning
When compiling a suspending proc body, the compiler splits at each suspension point: everything after becomes a continuation closure capturing live variables
Single await: code before await runs normally, code after becomes continuation closure capturing live locals, OP_AWAIT emitted with future + continuation
Multiple sequential awaits create chained continuations: each await's continuation contains the next await's continuation (nested closures)
Variable liveness analysis at each suspension point: only variables used after the point are captured by the continuation closure
Continuation closures use existing closure/upvalue compilation mechanism (nested Compiler context, upvalue resolution)
Non-suspending code before the first suspension point executes normally (no CPS overhead)
The __k continuation parameter is passed through: callers of suspending procs pass their own continuation

Direct-style suspension propagation: calling a suspending proc from any proc automatically makes the caller suspending and CPS-transformed — the call site passes the caller's __k to the callee. No explicit bridge needed
When top-level code is suspending (calls suspending procs or uses await/parallel/race directly), the compiler CPS-transforms it; the runtime provides __k = program completion handler

Unit tests: compile suspending procs with 1, 2, 3 sequential awaits; verify correct continuation closures with correct upvalue counts; verify non-suspending procs unaffected; verify call to suspending proc propagates CPS to caller
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: The CPS transform creates nested Compiler contexts for continuations — same mechanism as fn/proc body compilation. This means CPS doesn't require new runtime concepts, it produces ordinary closures. OP_AWAIT is emitted at suspension points (runtime behavior implemented in US-006). The __k parameter is a regular local variable at the bytecode level. Direct-style: calling a suspending proc is itself a suspension point — the CPS transform splits around the call and passes __k through.

userStories.title: CPS transform — control flow
userStories.description: As a developer, I need the CPS transform to handle suspension points inside control flow constructs so that await can appear in if/cond/match branches.
acceptanceCriteria: Suspension inside if branches: when any branch contains a suspension point, code after the if becomes a join continuation. All branches (suspending and non-suspending) flow into this continuation
Non-suspending branches call the join continuation directly with their result value (no suspension overhead for non-suspending paths)
Nested if with suspension: inner if's join continuation feeds into outer if's join continuation
cond (chained if) with suspension: same pattern — each branch routes to common join continuation
match with suspension: same pattern as if — each arm routes to common join continuation
Suspension inside let blocks: live variables from outer scope plus let bindings captured in continuation

Nested suspension in expressions: arguments containing await evaluated left-to-right, each creating a continuation — e.g., [f [await $x] [await $y]] becomes __await(x, fn(xval) { __await(y, fn(yval) { __k([f xval yval]) }) })
Verify compile-time error for suspension inside try/catch
Unit tests: suspension in if (both branches suspend, one suspends, neither), nested if, cond, match, nested await in call arguments, let block with suspension
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: The join continuation pattern ensures all branches of a control flow construct converge on the same continuation, regardless of whether individual branches suspend. This is the standard CPS transform for conditionals. The key insight: non-suspending branches become tail calls to the join continuation.

userStories.title: spawn primitive
userStories.description: As a developer, I need spawn to launch a closure as a concurrent task and return a future handle.
acceptanceCriteria: spawn recognized as builtin command by compiler; takes exactly 1 arg (zero-arg closure, suspending or non-suspending); NOT a suspension point

Add OP_SPAWN opcode: pop closure, create pending JaclFuture via gc_alloc, create task wrapper that executes closure on worker VM (passes __k=resolve_future if suspending, calls normally if non-suspending, catches errors via jacl_future_error), push task onto deque/inbox, push future onto stack
Calling a suspending proc directly propagates suspension to the caller via CPS transform — no explicit sync-to-async bridge needed (direct style)

Top-level suspending code (calls suspending procs or uses await/parallel/race) is CPS-transformed by the compiler; the runtime provides an implicit __k = program completion handler that signals the main thread

Runtime provides rt_run_to_completion(Runtime*, JaclClosure*, arena_t*) — submits the (possibly CPS'd) top-level closure as a task and blocks until the program completion future resolves. Used by vm_exec when top-level chunk is suspending

Unit tests: spawn returns future, spawned closure executes on worker, spawn with non-suspending closure resolves future with return value, spawn with suspending closure (closure containing await) resolves future correctly, spawn with error propagation
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: spawn creates a task wrapper (RuntimeTask) that wraps the user closure + future reference. For suspending closures, the wrapper provides __k = resolve_future(F) as the hidden continuation parameter. For non-suspending closures, the wrapper calls the closure directly and resolves the future with the return value. No run primitive — suspension propagates automatically through calls (direct style). Top-level async code just works.

userStories.title: await primitive
userStories.description: As a developer, I need await to suspend the current CPS continuation until a future resolves, then resume the next continuation with the result.
acceptanceCriteria: await recognized as suspension point by compiler (triggers CPS transform of enclosing proc); takes exactly 1 arg (a future value)
After CPS transform, await compiles to OP_AWAIT: pop continuation closure from stack (CPS-generated), pop future from stack

OP_AWAIT checks future state: PENDING → register continuation as waiter (jacl_future_add_waiter), return from vm__run; RESOLVED → schedule continuation as task on current worker's deque with result value, return from vm__run; ERROR → schedule continuation with M9 error value, return from vm__run
In all cases OP_AWAIT causes vm__run to return — current CPS segment is finished, worker picks up next task
When future resolves, all registered waiter continuations scheduled as RuntimeTasks on resolving worker's public deque with result as argument
Error model: await on errored future passes existing M9 error value (JaclVal with error tag) to continuation — user checks with error? predicate. No new error types introduced
Runtime error if await called with non-future value

Unit tests: await resolved future (immediate scheduling), await pending future (waiter registered, scheduled on resolve), await errored future (error value passed), multiple awaiters on same future, sequential awaits (chained continuations correct final result)
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: OP_AWAIT is the suspension mechanism — it causes vm__run to return, abandoning the current VM stack. All live state has already been captured in the continuation closure by the CPS transform. The worker's task loop then picks up the next available task. This integrates naturally with the existing Chase-Lev work-stealing infrastructure from M12.

userStories.title: parallel primitive
userStories.description: As a developer, I need parallel to fork N tasks and suspend until all complete, returning a vector of results in input order.
acceptanceCriteria: parallel recognized as suspension point by compiler; takes 2+ zero-arg closures; compile-time error if fewer than 2 arguments
After CPS transform, parallel compiles to OP_PARALLEL: pop continuation closure, pop N closures, create N futures + N task wrappers, push all tasks onto deques

Create GC-managed aggregate tracking structure (OBJ_PARALLEL_AGG): N individual futures, atomic completion counter, result slots array (N entries preserving input order), reference to join continuation
Each task wrapper on completion: atomically increment counter, store result at correct index. When counter reaches N, schedule join continuation with vector of all results
Result is JACL vector [result_0, result_1, ..., result_N-1] in input order (not completion order)
If any individual task errors, entire parallel errors: join continuation receives M9 error value (first error wins, subsequent errors discarded)
GC trace for OBJ_PARALLEL_AGG: trace all individual futures, result slots, and join continuation
Return from vm__run after OP_PARALLEL (suspension)

Unit tests: parallel 2 tasks (results in order), parallel 5 tasks, parallel with one error (aggregate errors), parallel with heavy allocation (GC stress), results preserve input order despite different completion times
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: The aggregate structure tracks completion atomically — each sub-task wrapper holds a reference to the aggregate and its index. When the last task completes (counter reaches N), it builds a JACL vector from the result slots and schedules the join continuation. First-error-fails-all matches Promise.all semantics.

userStories.title: race primitive
userStories.description: As a developer, I need race to fork N tasks and suspend until the first completes, returning the winner's result.
acceptanceCriteria: race recognized as suspension point by compiler; takes 2+ zero-arg closures; compile-time error if fewer than 2 arguments
After CPS transform, race compiles to OP_RACE: pop continuation closure, pop N closures, create N futures + N task wrappers, push all tasks onto deques
Create GC-managed race tracking structure (OBJ_RACE_AGG): _Atomic uint32_t settled flag (false initially), reference to race continuation, references to all N individual futures
Each task wrapper on completion: CAS settled from false to true. If CAS succeeds (winner), schedule race continuation with result. If CAS fails (loser), result discarded
Losing tasks run to completion — results silently discarded (no cancellation in M13)
If winning task errors, race continuation receives M9 error value
GC trace for OBJ_RACE_AGG: trace all individual futures and race continuation
Return from vm__run after OP_RACE (suspension)
Unit tests: race 2 tasks (faster wins), race returns winner's value, losers complete without crash, race with winning error (error propagated), race with concurrent GC
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: The CAS on settled ensures exactly one winner. Losers run to completion — their results become GC garbage. No cancellation in M13 (deferred to future PRD). The race continuation is scheduled by the winning task's wrapper, on the winning worker's public deque.

userStories.title: Remove VM stack root scanning from concurrent GC
userStories.description: As a developer, I need to remove VM stack root scanning from the concurrent GC path since CPS continuations capture all live state and VM stack scanning is not thread-safe (per GC_CONCURRENCY_DESIGN.md Section 7).
acceptanceCriteria: Remove VM stack scanning (stack[0..stack_top]) from gc_enumerate_roots in runtime.c
Remove call frame closure scanning from gc_enumerate_roots
Remove call frame chunk constant scanning from gc_enumerate_roots

Concurrent GC roots now exactly per GC_CONCURRENCY_DESIGN.md Section 7: (1) all tasks on all deques via snapshot, (2) each worker's currently_executing slot with BUSY sentinel, (3) global environment values, (4) intern table entries (Phase 1 immortal), (5) inbox tasks
Single-threaded GC path (gc_mark in gc_collect.c for non-runtime mode) retains VM stack scanning for backward compatibility with M0-M12 tests that don't use the runtime
All concurrency tests pass (CPS continuations capture all live state as task roots)
All M0-M12 tests pass (single-threaded path unchanged)
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: This completes the GC_CONCURRENCY_DESIGN.md Section 3 contract: continuation closures capture all live state, continuations are tasks on deques, GC scans deques. VM stack scanning was an M12 implementation shortcut that the CPS transform makes unnecessary and unsafe for the concurrent path.

userStories.title: Adaptive GC threshold
userStories.description: As a developer, I need the GC threshold to adapt based on survival rate so the collector runs less often when most objects are live and more often when there's lots of garbage.
acceptanceCriteria: Track bytes_survived during each GC sweep phase (sum of alloc_total for all live objects)
Track bytes_allocated since last GC (already tracked as bytes_since_gc)
Compute survival rate after each GC cycle: survival_rate = bytes_survived / bytes_allocated
Adaptive threshold adjustment: survival rate > 80% → increase threshold by 50%; survival rate < 20% → decrease threshold by 25%; otherwise no change
Configurable bounds: GC_THRESHOLD_MIN (default 256KB), GC_THRESHOLD_MAX (default 16MB). Threshold clamped to [min, max] after each adjustment
ThreadHeap stores gc_threshold (starts at GC_THRESHOLD default 1MB); gc_alloc compares bytes_since_gc against heap->gc_threshold instead of fixed GC_THRESHOLD
Works for both single-threaded (gc_collect) and concurrent (gc_concurrent_collect) paths
Unit tests: threshold increases after high-survival GC, decreases after low-survival GC, respects min/max bounds, threshold persists across cycles
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: This replaces the fixed 1MB threshold from M12. High survival rate means GC is wasting time re-tracing live objects — back off. Low survival rate means lots of garbage — collect more often. The adaptive heuristic is simple and effective; more sophisticated approaches (e.g., targeting a heap occupancy ratio) can be added later.

userStories.title: OOM escalation
userStories.description: As a developer, I need a 3-tier escalation when block allocation fails so the runtime can recover from transient memory pressure and fail gracefully under true OOM.
acceptanceCriteria: When gc_block_pool_get fails to allocate from OS: Tier 1 — emergency synchronous GC (single-threaded: gc_collect; concurrent: CAS gc_running, run gc_concurrent_collect inline, release gc_running; if another GC running, wait for it). Retry allocation after emergency GC
Tier 2 — heap growth: if emergency GC didn't free enough, attempt to allocate from OS up to GC_MAX_HEAP_BLOCKS (default 4096 blocks = 256MB). If under limit, allocate and return
Tier 3 — panic: if OS refuses or max heap reached, print diagnostic to stderr (current heap size, allocation request, survival rate, worker count) and abort()
GC_MAX_HEAP_BLOCKS configurable as compile-time constant
BlockPool tracks total_blocks_allocated for limit enforcement
Unit tests: simulate OOM with very small GC_MAX_HEAP_BLOCKS, verify emergency GC fires, verify tier 3 panic with diagnostic message
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: Emergency GC is rare — only fires under extreme memory pressure when the normal concurrent GC hasn't kept up. The 3-tier design from GC_CONCURRENCY_DESIGN.md Section 15: emergency GC → heap growth → panic. Most programs never hit tier 2 or 3.

userStories.title: Integration tests and stress testing
userStories.description: As a developer, I need comprehensive integration and stress tests validating the CPS transform, concurrency primitives, and GC under concurrent load.
acceptanceCriteria: Create test/test_m13.c with integration tests grouped by feature

CPS correctness (direct style): single await, multiple sequential awaits (chain of 3), await in if branches (suspending + non-suspending), await in nested expressions, deep continuation chain (5+ awaits), variable capture correctness, calling suspending proc from another proc (suspension propagation)

spawn+await integration: spawn+await returns correct value, multiple spawn+sequential await, spawn with heavy allocation (GC triggers), await already-resolved future (no deadlock), await errored future (error? checkable), multiple awaiters on same future
parallel integration: parallel 2 tasks results in order, parallel 5 tasks all correct, parallel with one error propagated, parallel with heavy allocation per task
race integration: race 2 tasks faster wins, losers complete without crash or leak
Direct-style integration: top-level code calling suspending procs runs to completion, nested suspending proc calls (A calls B calls await) propagate correctly, error propagation through CPS chain
Multi-threaded stress: 4+ workers spawning recursive tasks, heavy allocation with concurrent GC, parallel 20+ tasks, race 10+ tasks, mixed spawn/await/parallel/race workload
Memory bounded: sustained spawn/await workload with GC — heap block count stabilizes, doesn't grow without bound
Regression: all M0-M12 C unit tests and .jacl harness tests pass
Add test/test_m13.c to build.sh TESTS array with -lpthread
All existing tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: Follow existing test pattern: test_helpers.h, PrintCapture, TestEntry table grouped by US-XXX comments. Concurrency tests use rt_run_to_completion to block the test thread for deterministic output. Stress tests need generous timeout (60s+) for CI. Use -fsanitize=thread for data race detection and -fsanitize=address for use-after-free during development.

userStories.title: Extend harness for multi-threaded execution
userStories.description: As a developer, I need the .jacl test harness to support running tests with the runtime worker pool so that concurrency tests exercise real multi-threaded execution via rt_run_to_completion.
acceptanceCriteria: Add '# mode: concurrent' header directive to .jacl file format — when present, the harness uses runtime_init + rt_run_to_completion instead of plain jacl_run()
Without '# mode: concurrent', behavior is unchanged (uses jacl_run() for single-threaded execution)

The concurrent mode must: initialize a Runtime with worker threads, compile the source to get a CompileResult, handle top-level CPS (suspending code produces a closure), submit via rt_run_to_completion, capture print output via the same PrintCapture mechanism, and clean up with runtime_destroy
Print capture must work from worker threads — worker VMs must have print_fn / print_ctx set to the shared PrintCapture (with mutex protection since output from concurrent tasks may interleave)
The '# mode: concurrent' directive is parsed alongside existing '# expect:' / '# expect-error:' headers
Update build.sh harness entry to include -lpthread flag
All existing .jacl tests continue to pass unchanged
All tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: rt_run_to_completion takes (Runtime*, JaclClosure*, arena_t*) and blocks until the program completion future resolves. The harness needs to compile the source, detect if the top-level is suspending (via CompileResult.suspending), wrap in the CPS closure pattern, and submit. Look at how jacl_run in vm.c handles cr.suspending for the pattern to replicate. Worker VM initialization uses runtime__init_worker_vm which is internal to the runtime — the harness should use the public runtime_init / runtime_destroy API and let workers self-initialize.

userStories.title: Spawn and await e2e tests
userStories.description: As a developer, I need .jacl e2e tests for spawn and await so that the full pipeline from JACL source to concurrent execution is validated.
acceptanceCriteria: spawn_basic.jacl — spawn a simple computation, await it, print result (# mode: concurrent)
spawn_value.jacl — spawn returns a future, await extracts the value
spawn_multi.jacl — spawn multiple tasks, await each sequentially, print all results in order
spawn_nested.jacl — spawn a task that itself spawns and awaits an inner task
spawn_heavy.jacl — spawn a task with heavy allocation (vector/map construction) to exercise GC under concurrency (# mode: concurrent)
await_resolved.jacl — await a future that has already resolved (no deadlock)
await_error.jacl — spawn a task that errors, await it, check with error? predicate
All files in test/jacl/, all use '# expect:' headers, all pass via harness
All tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: JACL concurrency works single-threaded via jacl_run() (recursive vm__run for spawn) and multi-threaded via runtime. Tests without '# mode: concurrent' exercise single-threaded path; tests with it exercise the worker pool. Include a mix. Remember: suspending code at top level must be wrapped in 'proc main [] { ... }; main' pattern. Use to-string for typed numeric output. Helper procs must be defined at top level (not inside CPS-transformed proc bodies).

userStories.title: Parallel primitive e2e tests
userStories.description: As a developer, I need .jacl e2e tests for the parallel primitive so that fork-join semantics are validated end-to-end.
acceptanceCriteria: parallel_two.jacl — parallel with 2 bodies, print result vector
parallel_order.jacl — parallel preserves input order in result vector (not completion order)
parallel_error.jacl — one parallel body errors, result is error (first-error-wins), check with error?
parallel_with_await.jacl — parallel bodies that internally use spawn+await
parallel_concurrent.jacl — parallel with '# mode: concurrent' to verify real worker execution
All files in test/jacl/, all use '# expect:' or '# expect-error:' headers, all pass
All tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: Parallel returns a JACL vector of results. [parallel { expr1 } { expr2 }] is a single-line command form — JACL parser treats newlines inside [...] as statement separators, so multi-line parallel may cause parse errors. Use single-line format or the 'proc main' wrapper pattern.

userStories.title: Race primitive e2e tests
userStories.description: As a developer, I need .jacl e2e tests for the race primitive so that first-wins semantics are validated end-to-end.
acceptanceCriteria: race_basic.jacl — race two bodies, print the winner's result
race_error.jacl — race where the winning body errors, result is error
race_concurrent.jacl — race with '# mode: concurrent' for real parallel execution
All files in test/jacl/, all use '# expect:' headers, all pass
All tests pass (build.sh)
userStories.notes: In single-threaded mode, the first body always wins (sequential execution). In concurrent mode, the actual faster body wins — tests should account for non-deterministic winner by either making one body trivially faster or checking that the result is one of the expected values. The '# expect:' header is line-exact, so non-deterministic output needs careful test design.

userStories.title: Async error handling e2e tests
userStories.description: As a developer, I need .jacl e2e tests for error handling through async code paths so that error propagation via futures and CPS continuations is validated.
acceptanceCriteria: async_error_spawn.jacl — spawn a task that calls [error "msg"], await it, verify error? is true and error-val returns the message
async_error_propagation.jacl — error in a deeply nested async call chain propagates to the top-level awaiter

userStories.notes: JACL try/catch syntax is [try { body } e { handler }]. Suspension inside try/catch is a compile-time error — tests should NOT put await inside try. Error propagation through futures: jacl_future_error stores the error, await on an errored future passes the error value to the continuation.
